title: Static Variables
summary: Master shared class-level variables: lifecycle, memory allocation, global counters, and shared configuration flags.
learningOutcomes: Declare and use static variables for shared state and application-wide counters
Understand the static variable lifecycle from class load to JVM termination
Avoid common static variable concurrency and shared-state pitfalls

activities.title: Everyday Analogy: The Building Electricity Meter

analogy.story:
Imagine an apartment building with 20 flats.

Inside Flat 4B, the resident turns on their television. Inside Flat 2A, the resident turns on the air conditioning. Each flat has its own light switches and furniture (Instance variables).

However, in the basement of the building sits the Main Water and Electricity Meter (Static Variable). Every single apartment draws from the exact same water reservoir and main electrical line. When Flat 4B runs water, the main meter spins. When Flat 2A runs water, the exact same meter spins faster. There is only ONE meter for the entire building.

A static variable is that utility meter: a single, shared resource that all individual instances share and update together.
analogy.takeaway: Static variables provide a single source of shared truth for all instances of a class.

activities.title: Static Variable Lifecycle & Common Use Cases

concept.explanation:
A static variable (also known as a class variable) is declared using the 'static' keyword inside a class definition but outside any method.

Lifecycle:
1. Creation: Allocated in memory when the JVM first loads the class file into Metaspace.
2. Default Value: Primitives default to 0/0.0/false; object references default to null if not initialized explicitly.
3. Mutation: Any instance or static method can read or write to it. A change made anywhere is immediately visible to all instances everywhere.
4. Destruction: Reclaimed only when the ClassLoader unloads the class, which typically occurs when the JVM process shuts down.

Top 3 Practical Uses for Static Variables:
1. Object Counters: Counting how many instances of a class have been created.
2. Universal Constants: (When paired with 'final', which we cover in lesson 6) such as Math.PI.
3. Shared Configuration: Feature flags, database URLs, or default system currency.
rules: Rule 1: Use static variables when data is a property of the whole concept, not an individual entity.
Rule 2: Be cautious with mutable static variables in multi-threaded environments, as they can cause race conditions.
Rule 3: Static variables should rarely be declared public unless paired with 'final' to prevent rogue overwriting.

activities.content:
A static variable (also known as a class variable) is declared using the 'static' keyword inside a class definition but outside any method.

Lifecycle:
1. Creation: Allocated in memory when the JVM first loads the class file into Metaspace.
2. Default Value: Primitives default to 0/0.0/false; object references default to null if not initialized explicitly.
3. Mutation: Any instance or static method can read or write to it. A change made anywhere is immediately visible to all instances everywhere.
4. Destruction: Reclaimed only when the ClassLoader unloads the class, which typically occurs when the JVM process shuts down.

Top 3 Practical Uses for Static Variables:
1. Object Counters: Counting how many instances of a class have been created.
2. Universal Constants: (When paired with 'final', which we cover in lesson 6) such as Math.PI.
3. Shared Configuration: Feature flags, database URLs, or default system currency.


### Code Illustration:
```java
public class BankAccount {
    private int accountNumber; // Instance
    private static int nextAccountNumber = 1001; // Shared generator counter

    public BankAccount() {
        this.accountNumber = nextAccountNumber++; // Automatically generates 1001, 1002, 1003...
    }
}
```


### Core Rules:
- Rule 1: Use static variables when data is a property of the whole concept, not an individual entity.
- Rule 2: Be cautious with mutable static variables in multi-threaded environments, as they can cause race conditions.
- Rule 3: Static variables should rarely be declared public unless paired with 'final' to prevent rogue overwriting.

keyTakeaways: Rule 1: Use static variables when data is a property of the whole concept, not an individual entity.
Rule 2: Be cautious with mutable static variables in multi-threaded environments, as they can cause race conditions.
Rule 3: Static variables should rarely be declared public unless paired with 'final' to prevent rogue overwriting.

questions.prompt: What is the scope and lifetime of a static variable in Java?
questions.question: What is the scope and lifetime of a static variable in Java?
options: Created when a method is called; destroyed when the method returns
Created when 'new' is called; destroyed when the object is garbage-collected
Created when the class is loaded by the JVM; persists until the JVM shuts down
Created on every loop iteration
questions.explanation: Static variables have class lifetime: born upon class loading, living until JVM process shutdown.

questions.prompt: What is the default value of an uninitialized static int variable in Java?
questions.question: What is the default value of an uninitialized static int variable in Java?
options: null
undefined
questions.explanation: Like instance numeric variables, static numeric primitives default automatically to 0.

questions.prompt: Why should mutable static variables almost always be marked 'private'?
questions.question: Why should mutable static variables almost always be marked 'private'?
options: Because public mutable static variables act as dangerous global variables that any class can corrupt without validation
Because the compiler rejects public static variables
Because private variables run faster
To make them available to all threads
questions.explanation: Public mutable static variables are essentially uncontrolled global variables, which are prone to bugs and hard to trace.

questions.prompt: How can a class guarantee that each instantiated object receives a unique, sequential serial number?
questions.question: How can a class guarantee that each instantiated object receives a unique, sequential serial number?
options: By generating a random number in the constructor
By maintaining a private static counter and incrementing it inside the constructor
By asking the user to type in an ID
By using an instance variable
questions.explanation: A private static counter incremented in the constructor guarantees continuous sequential numbering across all instances.

questions.prompt: What is a 'race condition' when dealing with static variables in multi-threaded programs?
questions.question: What is a 'race condition' when dealing with static variables in multi-threaded programs?
options: When the CPU runs at maximum clock speed
When two or more threads attempt to read and write to the same shared static variable simultaneously, leading to corrupted data
When an object is deleted faster than expected
When a method returns before executing
questions.explanation: Race conditions occur when concurrent unsynchronized threads interleave reads and writes to shared memory.

questions.prompt: In our building utility meter analogy, what do individual apartments represent?
questions.question: In our building utility meter analogy, what do individual apartments represent?
options: Static variables
Instance variables and individual object instances
Static blocks
The operating system
questions.explanation: Each apartment is an individual object instance with its own private furniture (instance variables).

questions.prompt: If Class A has 'static int count = 0;' and 5 instances are created, each doing 'count++', what is count?
questions.question: If Class A has 'static int count = 0;' and 5 instances are created, each doing 'count++', what is count?
questions.explanation: Because count is static and shared, all 5 constructors increment the same counter, resulting in 5.

questions.prompt: Can a static variable be initialized with a complex expression or method call at declaration time?
questions.question: Can a static variable be initialized with a complex expression or method call at declaration time?
options: No, only constant literals (like 0 or 10) are allowed
Yes, you can initialize a static variable using any valid static expression or static method call
Only if the method is marked private
Only inside the main method
questions.explanation: Static variables can be initialized with static method calls or expressions (e.g. static long startTime = System.currentTimeMillis();).

questions.prompt: What happens if you try to use the 'this' keyword when initializing a static variable at class level?
questions.question: What happens if you try to use the 'this' keyword when initializing a static variable at class level?
options: It returns null
The compiler emits an error: 'cannot use this in a static context'
It defaults to the first object created
It creates an infinite loop
questions.explanation: 'this' represents the current heap instance, which does not exist in a static context.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of a static variable in Java's standard library?
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a static variable in Java's standard library?
options: System.out
Scanner.nextLine
String.substring
Math.random()
questions.explanation: System.out is a public static PrintStream field defined on the java.lang.System class.

questions.question: What is the difference between a static variable and an instance variable in Java?
questions.answer: An instance variable belongs to an individual object instance on the heap; each instance has its own copy. A static variable belongs to the class as a whole and exists as a single shared copy in Metaspace, accessible to all instances.
keyTakeaways: Instance = 1 copy per object in Heap
Static = 1 copy per class in Metaspace

questions.question: Why are public mutable static variables considered a major code smell?
questions.answer: Public mutable static variables are globally accessible mutable state. Any method anywhere in the application can overwrite their values without validation or audit trails, causing unpredictable side effects and making unit testing nearly impossible.

questions.question: How are static variables handled when a class is loaded by multiple ClassLoaders?
questions.answer: Static variables are scoped to the java.lang.Class object created by a specific ClassLoader. If two different ClassLoaders load the same class file, each ClassLoader creates its own distinct Class object and its own independent set of static variables.
keyTakeaways: Static state is scoped to the ClassLoader
Multiple ClassLoaders create multiple static copies

questions.question: Are static variables garbage collected in Java?
questions.answer: Static variables are referenced by their java.lang.Class object, which is referenced by its ClassLoader. As long as the ClassLoader remains reachable (which is true for system and application ClassLoaders throughout JVM execution), static variables are NOT garbage collected. Only if a custom ClassLoader itself becomes unreachable can its loaded classes and static variables be collected.
keyTakeaways: Persist as long as ClassLoader is active

questions.question: What is the thread-safety risk associated with 'count++' on a static variable?
questions.answer: The expression 'count++' is not atomic: it consists of three separate CPU operations (Read count, Add 1, Write back). If two threads execute this simultaneously, an interleaved read can cause one increment to be lost, resulting in incorrect counts.
keyTakeaways: Requires synchronization or AtomicInteger in concurrency

questions.question: Can a static variable be declared inside a local method in Java?
questions.answer: No. In Java, local variables inside methods cannot be marked static. The 'static' modifier is only valid for class-level members (fields, methods, blocks, nested classes).
keyTakeaways: No local static variables in Java

Each vehicle has private int vehicleId (instance, auto-assigned starting at 101) and private String status (instance, default 'AVAILABLE'). In Main, create 3 vehicles (all initially available). Dispatch vehicle 1. Print 'Available: 2, On Mission: 1'.
